prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators and its experimental realisation in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: Topological insulators replaced the symmetry-breaking picture of electronic phases with a classification by band topology, and the Kane-Mele Z2 invariant and quantum spin Hall proposal, followed by Molenkamp's transport observation in HgTe wells, give a clean chain from concept to measurement. Five of eight members placed it in their top three and all eight ranked it, which is the broadest support on the shortlist, but I rest the case on the science rather than the count. The work has been confirmed for nearly two decades in transport, ARPES and scanning probes across several material families, and it is the field where first-principles band-structure calculations and experiment have worked together most decisively. It extends the 2016 prize on topological phases to time-reversal-invariant systems rather than repeating it, because the new ingredient is spin-orbit-driven band inversion in a real material, not the integer quantum Hall or Haldane-type phases honoured then.
statement.case_against: The credited names are incomplete. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang made the HgTe prediction that told Molenkamp's group what to measure, and the 3D topological insulator work of Fu, Kane, Mele, Moore, Balents, Hasan and others lies outside the trio, so a three-person prize could be criticised as splitting a single discovery unevenly. The centre of gravity is also unsettled: citing the 2D quantum spin Hall effect honours the cleanest chain but leaves out the 3D materials that made the field broad, while a broader citation would exceed the supplied names. Practical applications remain limited, so the case is conceptual, and the cap of three laureates is a real constraint here.

responses.point: Kroll ranked optical lattice clocks (B022) first on the grounds that Katori's idea is simple, powerful and measurement-limited, with an excellent timing argument, and ranked B039 only eighth, citing strong confirmation but difficult allocation and his own limited ability to judge condensed-matter details.
responses.response: I take the clock case seriously. It has a clean two-person credit, which is its main advantage over B039, and I keep it as my first alternative. I disagree on ranking it above topological insulators. The allocation problem on B039 is real, but it concerns who is left out, whereas the three supplied names are each decisive for a distinct step: theory, experiment and the Z2 classification. The clock also sits close to the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-trap prizes, and the pending redefinition of the second is a maturity marker that topological insulators do not need. Kroll's own hesitation about condensed-matter detail is candid, and it is the reason I would ask him what specific allocation concern outweighs the theory-experiment chain.

responses.point: Danielsson ranked IceCube neutrinos (B003) first as a clear discovery that opened a new window, and placed B039 fourth, noting the omission of Zhang, Bernevig and Hughes and the overlap with the 2016 topology prize.
responses.response: I agree that the omission of the BHZ authors is the most serious weakness of B039, and I do not claim to resolve it from the supplied names. On the 2016 overlap I disagree: that prize honoured topological phase transitions and the quantum Hall and Haldane lineage, while the Z2 invariant, spin-orbit-driven band inversion and protected edge states in time-reversal-invariant materials form a distinct and later achievement. On B003, I accept the discovery is secure, but a one-name configuration for a collaboration-scale result is a weaker allocation than a three-person theory-plus-experiment prize, and Pearce's own opening says that a single laureate would be a thin summary of the credit. I would keep B003 off my configuration unless the committee finds a defensible way to widen the credit.

responses.point: Olsson ranked the quantum cascade laser (B001) first as a genuine invention in the statutory sense, with a clear Faist-Capasso-Cho split, and put B039 second, with the compound theory-plus-experiment-plus-3D structure as an allocation concern.
responses.response: The statutory invention argument for B001 is strong and its maturity is beyond question, so I keep it on my list of serious candidates even though it is not among my alternatives. My reservation is that its credit has its own gaps, namely the Bell Labs co-authors and the Kazarinov-Suris 1971 proposal that Johansson also flagged, and that it reads as engineering to some members. I agree with her that B039 combines parts that may deserve different recognition, which is why I propose a single citation anchored on the 2D quantum spin Hall effect with its HgTe realisation rather than a broad 'topological materials' wording that would invite the 3D credit question.

responses.point: Johansson ranked B039 first as an original, clear and overdue achievement, with Kane and Mele supplying the theory and Molenkamp the decisive observation, and noted that the BHZ and 3D priority questions rest on recollection.
responses.response: I agree on the substance and share the same caveat, since my knowledge of the BHZ and 3D priority history is also from memory and not checked against the record. I would add that agreement between members who rank this candidate first should not be read as settling the attribution issue. Where we may differ is what to do if the committee cannot accept the omission of BHZ: I would then prefer to narrow the citation to the Z2 and quantum spin Hall chain rather than add names, and I would want the committee to say so explicitly in round 2.

uncertainties: Whether the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang can be justified, given that the BHZ proposal directly guided the HgTe experiment.
Whether the citation should centre on the 2D quantum spin Hall effect or also cover 3D topological insulators, which would require names outside the supplied credit.
How the committee weighs closeness to the 2016 topological-phases prize, which I consider distinct but others may not.
Whether the optical lattice clock should be preferred if the SI second is formally redefined, which would remove its main maturity doubt.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile: none of the credited names for B039, B022 or B035 appears among my documented connections (my doctoral supervisor, Los Alamos colleagues, co-authors of my books and Uppsala Materials Theory colleagues). My research field, first-principles electronic structure and magnetism, is adjacent to topological band theory and I use it as a source of judgement, so I note that proximity as a possible bias towards condensed-matter candidates rather than as a recusal issue.
